name: Cosmetic leg lengthening (Precice nails)

lead: The Precice nail is an implant placed inside a long bone after the bone is cut. A magnet held outside the leg remotely lengthens the nail in small daily steps, so the bone grows longer without an external frame and height increases permanently. It was developed for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction and bone defects, and has been adopted for cosmetic lengthening in healthy adults.

The published literature is mostly case series and reviews in medical patients. Orthopaedic papers report accurate distraction and good bone healing. A 2025 meta-analysis compared external fixation with nailing for cosmetic lengthening, and a 2025 scoping review found studies capture clinical results better than quality-of-life outcomes.

paras: A surgeon cuts the femur or tibia and fixes the telescoping nail inside the canal; the patient then uses an external remote controller at home to lengthen it daily. Recovery involves weeks to months of limited weight-bearing and physiotherapy.

Reported problems include nail bending under load, failure of the bone to heal, joint stiffness and other complications, with some failures attributed to excessive loading. Surgeons describe it as demanding major surgery. Cosmetic use is elective and outside the device's usual medical indications.

angle.text: A magnetically driven nail inside the bone lengthens the leg in small steps without an external frame, adding permanent, measurable height. It is well studied for medical limb lengthening; cosmetic-specific data are newer.

lead: The Precice nail is a motorless, magnetically driven intramedullary (inside-the-bone) lengthening nail made by Ellipse Technologies, later NuVasive. An external remote control uses a magnet to lengthen the implant in small controlled increments after the bone has been cut, so the bone grows longer through distraction osteogenesis without an external fixator.[1] A 2014 study of the device noted that earlier internal lengthening designs had imprecise distraction, with nerve injuries, joint contractures and nonunion, and that the magnet-operated Precice nail had recently been cleared by the FDA.[2]

The nail is used for limb-length discrepancy, deformity correction, humeral lengthening and bone transport after tumour resection, and is also used in cosmetic stature lengthening.[3][4][5] Expert commentary describes strong bone healing with the retrograde femoral nail, and attributes the few failures to excessive loading of the limb and implant.[6]

Cosmetic lengthening is a smaller part of the literature. A 2025 meta-analysis of seven studies and 489 patients compared external fixation with intramedullary nailing and reported fewer problems and obstacles with nails, high satisfaction overall and no procedure-related deaths; a 2025 scoping review of 20 studies found outcomes dominated by clinical measures, with quality of life assessed in a quarter of studies.

For someone who wants to be taller, the draw is a permanent gain in bone length measured in centimetres, without the external frame that earlier cosmetic lengthening required. Surgeons and patients in cosmetic series describe gains of several centimetres from femoral or tibial lengthening, at the cost of weeks to months of limited weight-bearing and rehabilitation.[7] The practice is largely a medical-tourism and elective field, and case reports and reviews describe regulation as uneven.[8][9]

paras: After a precise bone cut (osteotomy), the nail is fixed inside the medullary canal with interlocking screws. Lengthening is performed gradually by an external remote controller; the 2014 evaluation assessed the accuracy and precision of distraction, effects on alignment and other outcomes.[2] The nail can also be shortened by remote control, a feature used in a case report to extend total lengthening in a 14 cm discrepancy.

Surgeons often combine the nail with blocking screws and temporary external fixation to correct alignment, and a 2018 series of 27 patients describes combining an external fixator with the retrograde Precice nail for simultaneous acute deformity correction and gradual lengthening.[6][10]

Distraction osteogenesis, the biological principle behind limb lengthening, was first proposed by Bernhard von Langenbeck in 1869, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, cutting the femur and applying traction through a pin in the heel bone with a high complication rate.[9] From the 1950s Gavriil Ilizarov studied the method in thousands of patients, developed external fixation devices and determined suitable separation rates, which led to widespread use of the Ilizarov apparatus, including for cosmetic lengthening.[9][7][11]

Internal lengthening nails sought to remove the external frame. A 2014 evaluation noted that earlier internal designs had imprecise distraction and complications including nerve injury, joint contracture and nonunion, and that the magnet-operated Precice nail, made by Ellipse Technologies (later NuVasive), had recently been cleared by the FDA.[2] A motorized implantable nail, Fitbone, from Wittenstein, is another internal option.[9] Post-market study NCT01601301 of the Precice system in 32 patients was registered in 2012.[12] A later device generation, the STRYDE nail, was compared with Precice in a 2023 single-centre matched-pair analysis of 42 STRYDE and 82 Precice patients treated between May 2013 and November 2020.[13]

sections.h: Origins and spread as a cosmetic option
paras: Cosmetic stature lengthening predates the magnetic nail. Before implantable nails, people seeking height relied on the Ilizarov external frame, and a 2005 series of 54 cosmetic bilateral leg lengthenings reported a mean gain of 7 cm with improvement in psychological problems tied to short stature.[7] Wikipedia notes that demand is strong in India, where height is linked in public perception with marriage and career prospects, and that China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after a series of operations caused serious side effects.[9]

The attraction of the magnetic nail is the absence of a frame: after the bone is cut and the implant locked, lengthening is performed externally with the remote magnet rather than by turning pins. A 2014 evaluation of the cleared device described this as addressing the imprecision, nerve injuries, contractures and nonunion of earlier internal designs.[2] As a result, nail-based cosmetic lengthening is discussed in height-surgery communities as the 'internal' alternative to external fixators, and the device's medical literature in children, adults and tumour reconstruction is frequently cited when people compare options.[1][4]

Authors describing the field call it part of orthopaedic cosmetic surgery tourism, with patients travelling for cost or access, and a 2024 JPRAS Open case report described a 28-year-old man who had bilateral lengthening in Turkey and then needed costly management of serious complications at home.[8]

People who pursue the procedure describe it as a permanent change to height measured in centimetres, and report in published series improvements in self-image tied to short stature.[7] Surgeons in published cosmetic series stress that candidates must be highly motivated and fully informed.[7] Proponents of nails over frames say the absence of pins reduces infection risk, scar tissue and the burden of pin-site care, a point also made for the motorized Fitbone implant.[2][9]

Critics inside orthopaedics argue that cosmetic outcomes are under-measured. The 2025 scoping review reported that only 25 percent of included studies assessed quality of life and 55 percent measured satisfaction, mostly with unvalidated tools, and called for standardized patient-reported outcome measures.

In general terms, the surgery involves a controlled bone cut in the thigh bone or shin bone, insertion of the implant in the canal, a waiting period, then daily external-magnet lengthening over weeks, followed by months of consolidation, physiotherapy and limited weight-bearing until the new bone strengthens.[2][10][14] Surgeons sometimes combine the nail with blocking screws or temporary external fixation to control alignment.[6][10] A case report describing a patient who intermittently bore weight against advice and fractured the nail illustrates why surgeons emphasise following the loading restrictions.[14] The nail can also be shortened remotely if needed.

Medical uses described in the literature include femoral and tibial lengthening in adults and children, treatment of limb-length discrepancy in fibular hemimelia (including combination with ACL reconstruction), humeral lengthening and bone-transport reconstruction after tumour resection.[3][4][15][16]

Cosmetic stature lengthening is performed for people of typical height who wish to be taller. Reviews of the cosmetic literature compare nails with external fixators and describe the older Ilizarov cosmetic experience, which a 54-patient series reported achieving a mean 7 cm of lengthening with improvement in psychological problems linked to short stature.[7]

A 2021 systematic review of Precice in children and adolescents included five studies with 131 patients and 135 femurs, evaluating clinical and radiological outcomes and complications. A 50-case paediatric series from a single institution and other retrospective series report outcomes in adults and young patients, and a 2020 paper reports results of the nail for adult limb-length discrepancy.[17][4]
Expert commentary credits the retrograde nail with strong bone healing after femoral osteotomy.[6]

In the 2025 meta-analysis, cosmetic lengthening with external fixation showed 56 percent Paley problems, 48 percent obstacles and 10 percent complications, versus 37 percent problems and 42 percent obstacles for intramedullary nailing with no significant complications reported, and satisfaction was generally high, up to 95 percent in external-fixation studies. The authors concluded both techniques are viable and recommended pairing surgery with psychosocial support.

Reported issues include nail bending and plastic deformity, studied in a 2024 paper on femoral lengthening, and the retrieval analysis of explanted Precice systems, which examined device wear and failure modes.[18] Expert accounts attribute the few failures to excessive loading of the femur and implant during treatment.[6]

Earlier internal lengthening devices were associated with imprecise distraction, nerve injury, joint contracture and nonunion, which the Precice design aimed to address.[2] Cosmetic-specific complication rates are the subject of a 2025 meta-analysis.

The 2023 matched-pair analysis reported osteolysis next to the telescopic junction in 65 percent of STRYDE segments compared with 1 percent of Precice segments, and implant failure in 19 percent of STRYDE and 9 percent of Precice nails, with breakage of distal locking bolts in 10 percent of STRYDE nails and none in the Precice group.[13] A 2023 case report described partial breakage of a Precice nail that had been reactivated for a second lengthening in a 21-year-old with a short tibia, late in consolidation; the patient had intermittently bearing weight against advice, and the nail was removed on an emergency basis.[14]

A 2014 paper asked about the risks of cosmetic lower limb lengthening by Ilizarov apparatus, which is the older benchmark that nail-based lengthening is compared with.[11] A 2024 case report described a 28-year-old man who had bilateral cosmetic lengthening in Turkey and developed serious complications, and the authors highlighted the lack of regulation and the cost of managing complications at home.[8]

Wikipedia's distraction osteogenesis article summarises general risk figures for limb lengthening, including infection in about 5 percent, bone healing in the wrong direction in 7 to 9 percent and hardware failure in 3 to 4.5 percent, though these figures cover lengthening broadly and not the Precice nail specifically.[9]

Published evidence consists of case series, reviews and technical notes. A 2025 meta-analysis of cosmetic limb lengthening compared external fixation and intramedullary nailing for complications and functional outcomes; a 2025 scoping review of 20 studies mapped outcome measures in cosmetic stature lengthening; and a 2021 systematic review covered five paediatric Precice studies. Single-centre series report Precice use in 50 children and adolescents, 27 patients with combined deformity correction, and adult discrepancies.[10][17][4]
Registered studies include post-market evaluations of the Precice system in 32 patients, and ongoing studies in children and in adults with limb-length discrepancy.[12][19]

A 54-patient series of cosmetic bilateral lengthening by the Ilizarov method reported a mean lengthening of 7 cm with a low complication rate, and good or excellent outcomes in all patients, including improvement in psychological disturbances related to short stature; the authors stated that candidates must be highly motivated and fully informed.[7] A 2023 matched-pair comparison of Precice and STRYDE nails, a 2022 review of Precice after tumour resection, and a 2023 Latin American series of Precice for post-traumatic bone defects add technical outcomes in medical patients.[13][1][20]

The 2025 scoping review identified 20 studies and 410 reported outcomes, found that 75 percent of outcomes were physiological or clinical, and noted that adverse events accounted for 3 percent of reported outcomes.

Wikipedia's distraction osteogenesis article notes that cosmetic limb lengthening is in demand in India, where height is associated with marriage and career prospects, that the industry there is described as unregulated, and that some patients as young as 13 or 14 have undergone the procedure, with reports of infection, reoperation and less height than expected.[9] China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening in 2006 after a series of operations caused serious side effects.[9]

Orthopaedic papers describe cosmetic stature lengthening as part of an emerging field of orthopaedic cosmetic surgery tourism, driven by cost and access.[8] A 2025 scoping review found that studies capture clinical results better than the life impact measures patients care about.

The device is discussed in height-surgery communities as the internal alternative to external fixators, with threads comparing the frame-free recovery, cost, destinations and surgeons. A T Nation thread on clavicle lengthening, a related distraction osteogenesis procedure, drew 155 posts in 2017.[21] See the limb lengthening surgery entry for forum discussion of cost, destinations and recovery.

lore.intro: Height-surgery communities discuss nail-based lengthening as the frame-free option, comparing cost, surgeons and destinations, while the orthopaedic literature supplies most quantitative claims. [21]

claims.claim: A nail gives a permanent gain of several centimetres without an external frame
Nails are safer than external fixators for cosmetic lengthening
Lengthening improves confidence and quality of life for short men
